content: While some countries already meet the necessary standards for TB surveillance, others face significant gaps, such as underreporting of cases diagnosed in the private sector or lack of access to healthcare for individuals with TB. It also aims to guide countries in strengthening their surveillance systems. The checklist includes two main parts: Part A provides a general description of the TB surveillance system being assessed, while Part B evaluates specific standards and benchmarks related to data quality, system coverage, and TB mortality data. Supplementary standards address TB/HIV coinfection, drug-resistant TB, and childhood TB. The checklist was developed by a core team of experts from WHO headquarters, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and other organizations, with input from various stakeholders and pilot testing in 11 countries, including Brazil, China, Kenya, and the United States. The tool underwent revisions based on these field tests. The checklist is designed to be used every three to five years and includes recommendations for corrective actions and estimated budgets to address identified gaps. Certification of a TB surveillance system requires meeting all 10 core standards and associated benchmarks, as well as supplementary standards for specific TB subpopulations. Certification provides an objective analysis of the system's current state and serves as a baseline for future improvements. The checklist can be used by national TB program staff for self-assessment, provided they have a thorough understanding of the system. It requires data collection from various sources, including electronic and paper-based systems, and may involve interviews with stakeholders. The process can take several weeks, depending on the availability and format of the data. The findings should be summarized and disseminated to inform improvements in the surveillance system. The document also emphasizes the importance of systematic data verification, quality assurance procedures, and regular feedback to lower reporting levels. It highlights the need for a long-term financial plan to support TB surveillance activities and recommends routine evaluation of the surveillance system. The checklist assesses various aspects of the system, such as the use of standardized data collection tools, the inclusion of all TB cases in national data, and the frequency of data transmission. It also evaluates the availability of training for staff involved in data collection and reporting. In summary, the checklist and user guide aim to strengthen TB surveillance systems worldwide by providing a standardized framework for assessment and improvement.
